ready1_open_rewrite.raw_question_text: As shown in the figure, the horizontal distance between teaching buildings $AB$ and $CD$ is $BD=a\,m$. At point $C$ on top of teaching building $CD$, the angle of elevation to point $A$ on top of teaching building $AB$ is measured to be $\alpha$, and the angle of depression to point $B$ at the bottom of teaching building $AB$ is measured to be $\beta$. What is the height of teaching building $AB$?
ready1_open_rewrite.raw_answer_text:
\textbf{Solution:} Construct $CE\perp AB$,\\
since $BD=a\,m$,\\
thus $CE=BD=a\,m$,\\
in $\triangle BCE$, $BE=CE\tan \beta = a\tan\beta$,\\
in $\triangle ACE$, $AE=CE\tan \alpha = a\tan\alpha$,\\
therefore $AB=a\tan\beta + a\tan\alpha$,\\
hence the height of $AB$ is $\boxed{a\tan\beta + a\tan\alpha}$.

ready2_open_rewrite.final_cot: Image description: On the left side of the figure is the taller teaching building AB, with A at the top and B at the bottom; on the right side is the lower teaching building CD, with C at the top and D at the bottom. B and D are on the same horizontal ground, and BD is marked as the horizontal distance between the two buildings. Dashed lines of sight are drawn from C to A and B respectively; at C, the angle of elevation toward A is marked as α, and the angle of depression toward B is marked as β. Reasoning: Draw a horizontal line through C intersecting AB at E, then CE is parallel to the ground BD, and the two buildings are vertical, so CE=BD=a. In right triangle BCE, the vertical side corresponding to angle β is BE, and the horizontal side is CE, therefore BE=CE·tanβ=a tanβ. In right triangle ACE, the vertical side corresponding to angle α is AE, and the horizontal side is CE, therefore AE=CE·tanα=a tanα. The height of teaching building AB is obtained by adding the lower segment BE and the upper segment AE: AB=BE+AE=a tanβ+a tanα.
